planting.note: Set bulbs shallowly, with the neck at or just above soil level, after danger of frost has passed; where winters drop much below freezing, lift and store the bulbs indoors over winter like a gladiolus corm.

directions: This Andean species is the true 'Peruvian daffodil' of horticulture, distinct from the more commonly offered Hymenocallis x festalis hybrids, and is prized for wide, heavily fragrant white flowers whose narrow reflexed tepals radiate out from a central trumpet like the spokes of a basket. Plant bulbs in rich, well-drained soil in a bright spot with some afternoon shade in hot climates, and keep them evenly moist through active spring and summer growth. After bloom, taper off watering as foliage yellows to let bulbs enter a natural rest, and in zones colder than 8 dig and store the bulbs in barely damp peat or vermiculite over winter. Established clumps resent frequent disturbance, so leave them undisturbed for several years to build up the offsets that produce the heaviest bloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant large bulbs with the neck at soil level after frost danger has passed, in a sheltered, warm bed or large container; this is one of the least cold-hardy Hymenocallis species and needs winter protection outside zone 9.

directions: Native to the Florida Keys and the wider West Indies, this evergreen spider lily carries some of the broadest, glossiest strap leaves in the genus and clusters of intensely sweet-scented white flowers with a faint green blush at the base of the cup. Give it warm, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture during the growing season, and full sun to light shade — plants grown in too much shade produce lush foliage but fewer flower scapes. It thrives in coastal gardens with salt-tolerant companions and also performs well as a large patio container specimen that can be moved under cover before any frost. Divide congested clumps only when flowering declines, since this species blooms best when its thick, fleshy roots are left undisturbed for several seasons.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile
